questions.q: What does the editorial mean by “planning based on remnants”?
options: Copying the plans of earlier generations
Not quite. The article says: Setting aside what has been lost and building wisely on what remains.
Planning only for the short term
Not quite. The article says: Setting aside what has been lost and building wisely on what remains.
Saving a little from every plan for later
Not quite. The article says: Setting aside what has been lost and building wisely on what remains.
Setting aside what has been lost and building wisely on what remains
Yes. Germany, Japan and Singapore are the examples.
questions.rationale: “The best principle in life is not to be concerned with what has been lost, but by planning wisely to avail of what is still extant.”

questions.q: The editorial quotes a Hindi maxim about one who runs after the whole and leaves the part. What happens to him?
options: He learns to want less
Not quite. The article says: He loses both the part and the whole.
He keeps the part but not the whole
Not quite. The article says: He loses both the part and the whole.
He loses both the part and the whole
Right. “All or nothing” goes against the law of nature.
He gains the whole in the end
Not quite. The article says: He loses both the part and the whole.
questions.rationale: “One who runs after the whole, leaving behind the part, loses both the part and the whole.”

questions.q: The article asks us to see the alternation of day and night as something more than routine. What is it?
options: A burden that divides our time
Not quite. The article says: A rare arrangement made for man’s benefit, calling for gratitude.
A rare arrangement made for man’s benefit, calling for gratitude
Yes. Other worlds have nothing like it.
An accident of astronomy
Not quite. The article says: A rare arrangement made for man’s benefit, calling for gratitude.
A cycle that will soon end
Not quite. The article says: A rare arrangement made for man’s benefit, calling for gratitude.
questions.rationale: “This unique ordering of day and night is God’s own doing, for the especial benefit of man, and we would do well never to lose sight of what an extraordinary blessing it is.”

questions.q: A guest raged at a lock, its maker and his host, when in fact he had been given the wrong key. What does the article draw from this?
options: Anger opens what patience cannot
Not quite. The article says: When doors will not open, the fault is usually an outdated approach of our own, not enemies outside.
Locks today are badly made
Not quite. The article says: When doors will not open, the fault is usually an outdated approach of our own, not enemies outside.
When doors will not open, the fault is usually an outdated approach of our own, not enemies outside
Well read. New locks need new keys.
Hosts should be more careful
Not quite. The article says: When doors will not open, the fault is usually an outdated approach of our own, not enemies outside.
questions.rationale: “Most of our afflictions are due to our failure to live up to the standard of the times… you just cannot unlock new locks with old keys.”

questions.q: “Created in the best of moulds, then cast down as the lowest of the low.” How does the article relate these words to reason and emotion?
options: Both lead to the same end
Not quite. The article says: Following reason raises a person; being ruled by emotion brings him down.
Neither is under human control
Not quite. The article says: Following reason raises a person; being ruled by emotion brings him down.
Following reason raises a person; being ruled by emotion brings him down
Correct. Freedom of choice works both ways.
Emotion raises a person; reason hardens him
Not quite. The article says: Following reason raises a person; being ruled by emotion brings him down.
questions.rationale: “The path of reason leads to success, but the path of emotions leads to disaster… Dealing with things emotionally is like mishandling glassware.”

questions.q: According to the verse quoted from the chapter Al-Mulk, why did God create death and life?
options: To punish the first human beings
Not quite. The article says: To test which of us is best in conduct.
To make people fear one another
Not quite. The article says: To test which of us is best in conduct.
To keep the world from becoming crowded
Not quite. The article says: To test which of us is best in conduct.
To test which of us is best in conduct
Yes. This world is a selection ground for Paradise.
questions.rationale: “God created death and life so that He might test you, and find out which of you is best in conduct.”

questions.q: What reason does the article give for a “love all” outlook?
options: Loving others makes them easier to lead
Not quite. The article says: Everything we use is the fruit of all humanity’s labour, so every other person is our benefactor.
People are all alike
Not quite. The article says: Everything we use is the fruit of all humanity’s labour, so every other person is our benefactor.
Everything we use is the fruit of all humanity’s labour, so every other person is our benefactor
Well reasoned. Judaism, Christianity and Islam all teach love even of an “enemy.”
Hatred is forbidden by law
Not quite. The article says: Everything we use is the fruit of all humanity’s labour, so every other person is our benefactor.
questions.rationale: “Every other person is your benefactor… All this was not the work of any single human being: all of humanity was involved in this process.”

questions.q: How, according to the article, does false pride arise from reading history?
options: By reading too many books
Not quite. The article says: By remembering the successes while forgetting the sacrifice that went before them.
By doubting what historians say
Not quite. The article says: By remembering the successes while forgetting the sacrifice that went before them.
By remembering the successes while forgetting the sacrifice that went before them
Right. Success always follows great sacrifice.
By studying other nations’ past
Not quite. The article says: By remembering the successes while forgetting the sacrifice that went before them.
questions.rationale: “If you think success should follow without sacrifice, you will develop false pride… it reported success but excluded the sacrifice preceding it.”

questions.article: The Young Are a Great Force for Good
questions.q: What combination does the article say makes a mission succeed?
options: The old deciding everything
Not quite. The article says: The energy of the young joined to the experience of their elders, with modesty on one side and respect on the other.
The energy of the young joined to the experience of their elders, with modesty on one side and respect on the other
Yes. Confidence is good; over-confidence is not.
The young acting alone
Not quite. The article says: The energy of the young joined to the experience of their elders, with modesty on one side and respect on the other.
Each generation working apart
Not quite. The article says: The energy of the young joined to the experience of their elders, with modesty on one side and respect on the other.
questions.rationale: “Senior people must share their experience and the younger generation must share its energy. This brings a healthy blend that ensures success.”

questions.q: The verse 33:35 lists qualities side by side for “men and women.” What does the commentary conclude?
options: The list applies only to the Prophet’s household
Not quite. The article says: The same virtues are asked of both alike, though they may show differently.
Men are asked for more than women
Not quite. The article says: The same virtues are asked of both alike, though they may show differently.
The same virtues are asked of both alike, though they may show differently
Well read. Ten qualities are named.
Women are asked for more than men
Not quite. The article says: The same virtues are asked of both alike, though they may show differently.
questions.rationale: “Just as these qualities are required of men, so also are they required of women. Although their manifestation may be different, the qualities are the same for both.”
